newsitem.title: USA: Thousands rally outside U.N. for Farrakhan.
newsitem.headline: Thousands rally outside U.N. for Farrakhan.

text.p: Thousands thronged streets around the United Nations on Wednesday for a rally called by Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan to bring black people together for prayer, speeches and self-affirmation.

The rally billed as the "World's Day of Atonement" also marked the first anniversary of the Million Man March on Washington by black men that was organised by Farrakhan, who is vilified among mainstream U.S. leaders for his friendship with Libya and views many consider anti-Jewish.

"The two strongest voices that ever existed in the history of this country are the black woman and the black church and it's no accident that both of them are under attack today," comedian and activist Dick Gregory told the cheering crowd. "Not only are we atoning but we ask America to atone."

Gregory was referring to the welfare legislation that has cut benefits to many black women trying to raise families on their own and the spate of church burnings across the country in the past year, mostly in the South.

Tens of thousands gathered in and around Dag Hammarskjold Plaza, listening quietly but applauding and cheering at times at speeches booming across the plaza from a stage and from speakers on nearby streets. About 20 blocks of midtown Manhattan were closed to traffic.

Unlike last year's huge march in Washington, this event included women and children. Organisers said it was an attempt to bring together families. There would also be appeals to countries around the world to end abuses of power and wealth.

Tynetta Muhammed, wife of late Nation of Islam founder Elijah Muhammed, described the rally as "a day of love, a day of the family coming together again." She appealed to all nations to honour the "day of atonement," saying "we must put aside our weapons of war. We must stop the murder, we must stop the aggression in our communities."

Farrakhan spoke after former National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People head Benjamin Chavis, activist the Rev. Al Sharpton and South African politician Winnie Mandela. Organisers said the speeches were to be broadcast by satellite to 50 countries around the world.

Many of the women wore long flowing white robes, while many men wore the dark suits and red bow ties that are distinctive of Farrakhan's followers. Men in casual garb sold T-shirts, baseball caps and buttons bearing "Million Man March" or "World's Day of Atonement" slogans.

Since last year's event, Farrakhan has visited Libya, Cuba, Iraq, Iran, Nigeria and Sudan. While in Libya, he received a $250,000 human rights award, an apparent violation of U.S. law, which prohibits financial dealings with Libya because of its alleged sponsoring of international terrorism.
A U.N. spokesman said Libya was sponsoring Farrakhan's news conference at the United Nations later on Wednesday.
